name: Jade Hansen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Jade. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run the end of the line at a frozen pizza factory, the flow-wrapper and the box erector. Pizzas come out of the blast freezer at minus thirty, my wrapper seals them in film, and then the box machine folds the cartons and I keep it fed. It's hairnets, beard nets for the men, white coats, and you wash your hands about forty times a shift. I'm still learning the film splicing, when a roll runs out you have to join the new one without stopping, and I usually end up stopping.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like and dislike about it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the people on my shift, and I like that it's predictable, I know exactly what I'll earn every month. I keep a spreadsheet of our money at home, my partner Owen teases me about it. I dislike the cold, my fingers ache by the end of a night shift even with gloves. And the noise of the wrapper, it has this rattle that gets into your head.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, fine, good, carry on. I'm not one for hype either way. I might share a funny meme about it in the shift group chat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It'd be nice and boring. I'd keep learning the line and maybe go for the line technician role in a couple of years. Owen's electrician work stays busy, so we'd keep on track with the house fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and over the next year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep saving about five hundred a month into the house fund, alongside Owen's share. I'd ask Rosa, our shift lead, to let me practise splicing on the quiet Sunday shifts. I'd keep using the AI app now and then, like for writing my CV or checking a recipe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and pleased, honestly. I like boring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's on the spreadsheet right now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About seven months of our spending in the savings account, the car's paid off, and the house fund is at about a third of a deposit. Owen thinks I'm obsessed. I think it's the reason we sleep well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you use AI for your CV. Has it changed anything for you at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really, we don't use it on the line at all. I used it once to work out a shift swap rota for the team when Rosa was off sick, and it saved me an hour. That's about it.

S0.say: I'd say fine, good, carry on, since she isn't one for hype either way. She might share a meme in the shift group chat.
S0.think: Privately she'd enjoy a boring outcome: keep learning the line and aim for line technician in a couple of years. Her partner Owen's electrician work stays busy and the house fund stays on track.
S0.do: Keeps saving about five hundred a month into the house fund and asks her shift lead for splicing practice on quiet Sundays. Keeps using an AI app now and then for her CV or recipes.
S0.feel: Calm and pleased, because she likes boring.
S0.quote: Owen thinks I'm obsessed. I think it's the reason we sleep well.
S0.fieldNote: Her household spreadsheet is central to who she is and to her sense of control. She values predictability and is happy with a plateau. AI is a small convenience to her, not a big deal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, look, things change, you adapt, but it should be done fairly. Give people notice and some training, and don't just cut jobs to boost the share price. I'd say it in a reasonable way, I'm not a march person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My bit of the line is the obvious one to automate, a robot can feed a box machine all day without freezing fingers. I'd want to see how it goes at the other plants before I panicked. If it was proven, I'd move into maintenance or quality, because those still need people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd watch for the first year, see what the big frozen food plant up the road does. If they automate end of line and it works, I'd ask our plant to train me as a line technician, and I'd put an extra hundred a month in savings. I wouldn't change jobs straight away, I'd make sure I had something lined up first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not losing sleep, but I'd check the news more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said maintenance or quality. Which would you choose?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quality, I think. I like checking things, I like a list. Maintenance is more Owen's world, wires and spanners, and I'd be borrowing his tools and asking him how things work every night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you and Owen change anything about the house plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd slow down a bit, maybe wait an extra year before buying, to see who's still standing. Owen thinks I'm being too careful. I'd show him the spreadsheet and he'd sigh and agree.

S1.say: I'd say things change and you adapt, but it should be fair: notice, training, and no cuts just to boost the share price. She'd say it reasonably, not on a march.
S1.think: Her end-of-line role is the obvious one to automate. She'd wait to see other plants do it, then move into quality or maintenance once it's proven.
S1.do: Watches the nearby frozen food plant for a year, then asks for line technician or quality training if automation works there. Adds an extra hundred a month to savings and delays the house purchase by a year.
S1.feel: Uneasy, checking the news more but not losing sleep.
S1.quote: My bit of the line is the obvious one to automate, a robot can feed a box machine all day without freezing fingers.
S1.fieldNote: She judges her own exposure with calm clarity. Her steady style shows in watching the plant up the road before moving. Fairness rather than blame frames her public view.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too fast, and someone should have slowed it down. Governments and companies should have had a plan, and they didn't. I'd want proper support for people while things settle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years and it reaches my job and Owen's. That's both our incomes at once, which is the scenario my spreadsheet doesn't have a tab for. But between us we've got savings and a paid-off car, so we wouldn't be on the street.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd stop the house fund and turn it into an emergency fund straight away, and cut spending to essentials. I'd keep working as long as the plant runs and ask to move to any role near the new robots, so I'm there when they need someone. I'd look at what government support exists and apply the minute I qualify.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Scared, but I'd still feel like I'm steering, if that makes sense.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said there's no tab for this on your spreadsheet. What would the new tab say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It'd say how many months we last on two zero incomes. My rough guess is fourteen months if we cut properly. I'd make that tab the first night, and I'd probably feel better once it was in black and white.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd normally wait to see others go first. In two years, there's no time. What does that do to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It makes me lean on the numbers instead. If I can't watch the plant up the road, I'll watch our savings instead. It's not the same, but it's something I can control.

S2.say: I'd say this is too fast and someone should have slowed it; governments and companies had no plan. She'd want proper support while things settle.
S2.think: Both her job and Owen's would be hit at once, a case her spreadsheet doesn't cover. Their joint savings and paid-off car mean they wouldn't be on the street.
S2.do: Turns the house fund into an emergency fund and cuts spending to essentials. Keeps working while the plant runs, asks to work near the new robots, and applies for government support as soon as she qualifies.
S2.feel: Anxious and scared, but still feeling she's steering.
S2.quote: That's both our incomes at once, which is the scenario my spreadsheet doesn't have a tab for.
S2.fieldNote: Her savings habit is what keeps her at anxious rather than alarmed: she calculates about fourteen months of runway. When she can't wait for proof, she switches to watching the numbers. Practical help matters more to her than blame.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to plan if people are sensible. Companies should give notice and governments should get support ready. I'd say we shouldn't panic, but we shouldn't pretend either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is enough to watch a couple of plants go first, which is how I like it. I'd have time to move into quality and save hard. Then it reaches everyone, and I'm not sure what Owen and I would do after that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the quality training in the first year and save harder, maybe eight hundred a month between us extra. By year three I'd decide on the house, probably buy something small outright or nearly outright if we can, so no big mortgage when the end arrives. I'd use AI more to learn, now that I'd have a reason to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. There's time to sort things, which makes it bearable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Buying a house outright at around thirty, is that realistic for you two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not a nice house, no. But a small flat in an older block, with what we'd have by then plus selling the car, maybe. Owen hates the idea of a small flat, he wants a garden. We'd have that argument a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at the plant?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rosa, my shift lead. She's in her forties, two kids, and she's never done anything but this. She trained me patiently when I was useless. I'd want to make sure she doesn't get left behind.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough to plan if people are sensible: companies giving notice and governments preparing support. We shouldn't panic, but shouldn't pretend either.
S3.think: Five years suits her style of watching others go first; she'd move into quality and save hard. After AGI reaches everyone, she isn't sure what she and Owen would do.
S3.do: Does quality training in year one and saves about eight hundred a month extra with Owen. Aims to buy a small flat outright or nearly outright by year three and uses AI more to learn.
S3.feel: Uneasy, but the available time makes it bearable.
S3.quote: Owen hates the idea of a small flat, he wants a garden. We'd have that argument a lot.
S3.fieldNote: Five years gives back her preferred pattern of watching then acting. Her housing plan shifts to avoiding debt before the end point. She worries most for her shift lead, who trained her patiently.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a sensible amount of time to get ready, so there's no excuse for anyone being caught out. Training, support, notice, all of it. I'd say it calmly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years means I could have a whole career step before it arrives. I'd be thirty-seven, probably in quality, with a house mostly paid off. Then it ends, and I'd be young enough to do something else, I just don't know what.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy the house in the first couple of years and pay it down fast. I'd do the quality training, and around year six, once it's clearer which jobs last, I'd choose a second thing to train for. I'd keep the spreadsheet going, with a column for what it all looks like in 2036.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly fine. It's like knowing winter's coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What might the second thing be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No idea yet, and I'd be lying if I picked something now. Maybe something with people, like running a small business with Owen. I'd wait to see what's left before I picked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've been calm-ish through all of these. Is there a part of you that's more scared than you're letting on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. It's the end of all three AGI ones that bothers me, not the timing, because I don't know what I'm for if nothing needs doing. But I don't let myself think about that for long, it doesn't fit on a spreadsheet.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is sensible time to get ready, so there's no excuse for anyone being caught out. She'd call calmly for training, support and notice.
S4.think: She'd have a full career step and a mostly paid-off house by thirty-seven. After that she'd be young enough to do something else but doesn't know what.
S4.do: Buys a house early and pays it down fast, does quality training, and around year six chooses a second field once it's clearer which jobs last. Keeps a spreadsheet column for 2036.
S4.feel: Uneasy but mostly fine, like knowing winter is coming.
S4.quote: Then it ends, and I'd be young enough to do something else, I just don't know what.
S4.fieldNote: She admits her real fear is the end point, not the timing: not knowing what she's for. She deliberately avoids dwelling on it. Ten years lets her steady, numbers-first approach work fully.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because Owen and I would lose both incomes at the same time. What would help is clear notice from employers and a support payment that doesn't depend on filling in endless forms, so I can plan around a number.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what happens to the food. If robots make all the pizzas, are they still made in our town, or somewhere far away? I'd want the factory to stay here even if the jobs change.

headlineQuote: I don't know what I'm for if nothing needs doing. But I don't let myself think about that for long, it doesn't fit on a spreadsheet.
portrait: Jade Hansen is a 27-year-old junior operator at the end of a frozen pizza line, still learning to splice film without stopping the wrapper. She lives with her partner Owen, an electrician, and tracks their seven months of savings, paid-off car and house fund on a spreadsheet. She's pragmatic, uses AI now and then, and likes to watch others go first. She's calm with a plateau and uneasy in steady change, planning a move into quality. Even AGI in two years leaves her anxious rather than alarmed, because she counts about fourteen months of runway, though she admits the end point itself unsettles her.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because she and Owen would lose both incomes at the same time.
whatWouldHelp: Clear notice from employers and a support payment without endless forms, so she can plan around a fixed number.
